tier_reason: The numbers come from Table 2 of the peer-reviewed PVLDB 14(1) paper 'Benchmarking Learned Indexes' (Marcus et al.): IBTree 446.55 ns / 9.0 MB against the STX BTree at 482.11 ns / 166.0 MB, on a Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz. It is B, not A: the SOSD harness is public (learnedsystems/SOSD benchmarks/ + competitors/interpolation_btree.h + scripts/prepare.sh + CMakeLists.txt), but neither the paper nor the repo names the compiler. This matches the earlier B verdicts on RMI, RadixSpline and FAST from the same table.

corrections.workload: SOSD 'Benchmarking Learned Indexes' Table 2: the fastest configured variant of each structure, lower-bound lookups (10M random lookup keys) on a 32-bit version of the amzn dataset (200M keys). It is 32-bit because the SIMD CuckooMap in the table only supports 32-bit keys (footnote 4).
corrections.claimed_speedup: 446.55 ns vs the STX BTree's 482.11 ns lookup time (~1.08x, ~8% faster), using 9.0 MB vs 166.0 MB (~18x smaller) (derived from page data; 32-bit amzn, PVLDB 14(1) Table 2)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated in the paper or the repo (the README dependency list installs clang). SOSD CMakeLists.txt adds -ffast-math -march=native (and -fopenmp if available), and scripts/prepare.sh builds with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG).
corrections.caveats: Single table row: 32-bit amzn only, best variant per structure. The margin over the STX B-tree is modest (~8%). FAST (435.33 ns) edges it, and learned indexes (RMI 180.90 ns, RS 266.58 ns) and hash tables are far faster in the same table. IBTree is a header inside the SOSD benchmark repo, not a standalone library. SOSD has had no commits since April 2022. The previously cited CIDR'21 Hist-Tree paper does not contain IBTree or these numbers.

notes: The record's benchmark_url (Crotty, CIDR'21 Hist-Tree) evaluates BS/STX/ART/RMI/PGM/RS/HT/CHT on a c5.4xlarge Xeon Platinum 8124M with gcc 9.3.0. It never mentions IBTree, and it has no 446.55/482.11 numbers. The numbers, the table and the Xeon Gold 6230 hardware are all from the SOSD PVLDB paper (arXiv 2006.12804), so benchmark_url was corrected. Metadata checked: GPL-3.0, 313 stars, not archived; default-branch last commit 2022-04-08 (pushed_at 2022-04-27).

tier_reason: The Dec 17 2025 article states GCC -O3, an Intel Core i7-11700K, the OS/kernel and RocksDB v10.7.5, and links a raw report (benchmark_results_tdb610_rdb1075_range_seek1.txt) whose SEEK throughputs (3729450 vs 893870; 8867103 vs 1869637 ops/sec) match. The linked code, github.com/tidesdb/benchtool, is now 404. Its full history survives in the mirror dhoard/tidesdb-benchtool (commits by the TidesDB author, including 2e0d4b9d of 2025-12-16), so the code is public: tidesdb_rocksdb.sh test 11 'Seek Performance' plus engine_rocksdb.c / engine_tidesdb.c.

corrections.workload: benchtool tidesdb_rocksdb.sh: 8 threads, 16-byte keys / 100-byte values, sync disabled. Random and sequential seeks are 5M ops after populating 5M keys; Zipfian seeks run over ~650K unique keys; range queries of 100 and 1000 keys (random) and 100 keys (sequential). TidesDB v6.1.0 vs RocksDB v10.7.5.
corrections.caveats: First-party vendor benchmark by the TidesDB author. The official benchtool repo (github.com/tidesdb/benchtool) now returns 404, and the code survives only in the mirror dhoard/tidesdb-benchtool. TidesDB uses 3.46x more memory (851 MB vs 246 MB peak RSS) because it keeps SSTable metadata resident. Large 1000-key ranges are essentially a tie (1.11x, within variance per the author). In the raw report the seek phase logs 'tidesdb (v6.0.2)' and RocksDB 'vunknown'. TidesDB is an LSM key-value storage engine rather than an index structure.

notes: All claimed ratios and throughputs appear verbatim on the article (sequential 100-key ranges are an extra 1.14x). Metadata checked: MPL-2.0, 567 stars, not archived, not a fork; default-branch last commit 2026-09-25 (pushed_at 2026-09-26). Category 'indexes' is a loose fit for an LSM KV engine, but it cannot be corrected via this schema.
